rv.q: On a purely human one, this is the most thrilling and visceral drama. Not a minute wasted, not a beat missed. No less than a white knuckle ride.
There is surely no more effective manipulator of mood and pace working in British theatre today.

Yes, The Guilty is fairly straightforward as a text. Concerning a troubled police call centre operator, it’s writer Chloe Moss’s adaptation of the Danish film Den Skyldige and its Jake Gyllenhaal-starring Hollywood remake. You could probably have a fairly good time taking a version to the Edinburgh Fringe.
The Guilty is a masterclass in tension and control.
A step above the film, this is a gripping, high-stakes triumph – more than worth leaving the sofa for.

Then a call comes in that quickly changes his attitude; Emily is a victim of an apparent abduction, speaking to Joe from the back of a vehicle in a terrified whisper. As he scrambles to help her, the production escalates into a darkly compelling and propulsive thriller, complete with shocking climax.
I couldn't suspend my disbelief, so I was always distanced from what is undoubtedly an extraordinarily gripping and clever piece.
This is an anxiety-inducing 70 minutes that rarely lets the audience relax.

cn.t: Russell Tovey commands attention in this claustrophobically tense 70-minute thriller that delivers nail-biting anxiety. Critics praise the gripping tension and intimate staging, though some question whether it surpasses the existing film versions.
